LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

I Feel, I Need, I Want & I Choose — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson hands your child the four sentences that start with I — a voice that speaks feelings, needs, wishes and decisions without grabbing, hitting or whining.

What is this?

I feel names the weather inside, I need asks for what would help, I want speaks the honest wish and I choose owns the decision — four sentence-starters that carry a whole voice.

What does it mean?

I-statements are the peaceful alternative to grabbing, hitting and whining — the same message with the fighting stripped out. A child with I-words stops needing behaviour as a language.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: I FEEL is about inside weather (not "you made me" — just "I feel"); I NEED and I WANT are different (needs help, wants wishes — both allowed, said differently); and I CHOOSE is the proudest one — it means the decision is yours to own.

Why this matters

This card equips the check-in with sentence-starters: noticing and naming feelings (earlier cards) become SPEAKABLE sentences here. It is also the quiet alternative to every power struggle in the day.

What it teaches

Assertive communication (the healthy middle between passive and aggressive), needs-versus-wants differentiation, ownership language, and emotional expression in sentence form — the vocabulary of the whole class, armed with grammar.

Words to learn

I feelI needI wantI chooseI-statementmy voiceown it

Say this to your child

“"You have four magic sentence-starters, and every one begins with I. I feel — the inside weather: I feel sad, I feel excited, I feel that wobbly something. I need — what would help: I need a hug, I need help with the zip, I need you to listen. I want — the honest wish: I want the blue cup, I want a turn — wants are allowed; we just say them instead of grabbing them. And I choose — the proudest one: I choose this book, I choose to share. Four starters. When your words start with I, people lean in to listen — because you sound like someone who knows their own heart."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four sentences that start with I — your biggest voice."
  2. Read the panels: the chin-thinking girl says I FEEL, the open-armed boy says I NEED, the plain-spoken boy says I WANT, the confident girl says I CHOOSE.
  3. Model one of each, honestly: "I feel tired. I need five quiet minutes. I want tea. I choose the sofa."
  4. Play the I-statement dinner game below — one sentence per starter, everyone, grown-ups included.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "sentences that start with I are yours — nobody can interrupt your inside weather."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the I-statements: I Feel, a thoughtful girl with a hand to her chin; I Need, a boy explaining with open arms; I Want, a boy saying it plainly with crossed arms; and I Choose, a confident girl with a hand on her chest — a whole voice, drawn in four poses.

Ask your child

"Which starter talks about inside weather?" "What is the difference between a need and a want?" "Which starter owns the decision?" "What is YOUR I-feel right now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I feel… jumpy!" "I need help, please" or the owned one: "I choose the green one."

Out in the real world

I-statement moments appear all day: the blocked view at the fence (I need to see too), the feared haircut (I feel scared), the shared crayon (I want a turn next), the outfit standoff (I choose the dinosaur shirt). Grown-ups who use them out loud — "I need ten quiet minutes, then I am all yours" — hand over the grammar for free.

Try it together

The I-Game at Dinner: four rounds, one per starter. Round one: everyone says an I-feel (real or silly). Round two: an I-need. Round three: an I-want — no judgement, wishes are wishes. Round four: an I-choose (about something small and real: tomorrow’s breakfast, the walk route). Grown-ups go first each round — especially with one real "I need five quiet minutes", which lands funnier than any lecture.

Understanding check

Ask: "What starts every sentence today? Which one is the proud owner one? Are wants allowed?" I, I choose, yes — three answers and the small person has a big voice.

Parent tips

Coach the difference without the lecture: needs and wants both get said, but needs get met faster — "you NEED a band-aid, you WANT more pudding; the band-aid is coming, the pudding is a maybe." And when the I-feel names YOU as the villain ("I feel angry AT YOU"), accept the feeling, reroute the sentence: "I hear angry. And I feel — what else? …worried? tired? Let us start there." The I stays; the blame goes.

This lesson pairs with the I Feel, I Need, I Want & I Choose flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
